title: What the Reading Achievement Gap is Made Of
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: O'Brien, a district leader reading Ohio's report cards, argues that the annual fight between the poverty camp and the performance camp is unresolvable because the proficiency number they are arguing over contains two different things. He splits it: decoding is a threshold a school can install on its own within two years, while knowledge is a rate that accumulates over a decade mostly outside the classroom and compounds. He points out that the famous claim that 95 percent of children can learn to read is a claim about decoding by the end of first grade, explicitly exempting reasoning and listening comprehension, while state tests measure only comprehension. The Ohio data he reconstructs shows the poorest and wealthiest schools converting roughly similar numbers of off-track children, but a slippage between word reading and proficiency that widens from three points in the wealthiest fifth to twenty-nine in the poorest. For the source of the knowledge advantage he rejects museums and tutoring and lands on conversational turn-taking about things that are not in the room, citing the MIT study in which low-income children with high turn-taking matched high-income peers in language scores and brain activity. He then traces parent education back through segregation and redlining, arguing the gap is inherited rather than earned and therefore interruptible. His recommendations follow the split: own decoding completely with no poverty defense, build knowledge deliberately through a protected K-8 sequence, and stop reporting the two as one figure. He also indicts his own profession for buying reading minutes with science and social studies time, a trade high-poverty districts made at roughly twice the rate of wealthy ones.
points: The Moats statistic is habitually quoted only halfway, and the omitted clause is precisely the part that state tests measure.
Because knowledge compounds, a decoding fix produces the familiar jump from ten to forty percent proficient and then a plateau that gets misdiagnosed as a failure of will.
The MIT turn-taking finding matters practically because conversation is a teachable practice, whereas a parent's credential is not something a school can supply.
Using suburban proficiency as an annual verdict rather than a ten-year destination produces exactly the behavior, cutting content time for reading blocks, that guarantees the standard is never met.
He cites the Tennessee pre-K randomized study, where early gains faded and sixth graders fared worse than non-attenders, as the same error committed earlier in the pipeline.
quotes: Louisa Moats actually puts it this way: 95 percent of children can be taught to read by the end of first grade, with future achievement constrained only by their reasoning and listening comprehension abilities.
So for twenty years we have been holding a decoding promise up against a comprehension result and calling the difference poverty, or incompetence, depending on where we happen to sit.
Decoding is a threshold. The code is finite, a fixed body of sounds and letters and how they go together, and a child either has it or is on the way to having it.

Knowledge is a rate. Vocabulary and background knowledge are unbounded. They accumulate in thousands of small unplanned moments across years, nearly all of them outside a classroom, and they compound.

That's the whole argument, sitting in a state spreadsheet. Reading the words is one job. Understanding them is a different job. We have been funding schools for the first and grading them on the second.
What predicted their language skills wasn't how many words they'd heard. It was conversational turns, the back-and-forth, one person and then the other, over and over.
Read that again slowly. The schools whose children most needed knowledge from school cut the knowledge out of the schedule. The schools whose children were already getting it at home kept theirs.
Think about what that means. The standard produces the exact behavior that prevents anyone from ever meeting the standard.
